title: Vision-Based Gesture Control for Industrial Automation: A Review of MediaPipe Hand Landmark Recognition and Human–Robot Interaction

authors.name: Dr. Marco Rossi
authors.affiliation: Automation and Robotics Laboratory, Politecnico di Milano

abstract: Vision-based gesture control has emerged as a practical alternative to teach pendants, physical buttons, and voice control in modern industrial settings. Existing solutions often trade off recognition accuracy, latency, or safety certification when deployed near heavy machinery. This review examines MediaPipe Hands and related hand-landmark recognition approaches within the context of human–robot interaction (HRI) for factory automation. We analyze detection performance, feature normalization, temporal filtering, and integration with PLCs over Profinet in a laboratory installation at the Automation and Robotics Laboratory, Politecnico di Milano. Key quantitative observations from reproduced experiments show a reproducible gesture recognition accuracy of 95.4% and end-to-end command latency of 12.3 ms on an Intel i7 edge node, with throughput 81.3 FPS and a safety-critical latency budget of 50 ms. The paper provides detailed system architecture, algorithmic formulas for landmark normalization and Kalman smoothing, practical integration notes for ABB IRB 1600 robots and Siemens S7-1500 PLCs, and a comparison with template, HOG+SVM, and CNN baselines. We conclude with deployment recommendations, known limitations (occlusion, reflective surfaces, extreme illumination), and prioritized future work to address certification and multi-operator scenarios.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: Industrial manufacturers increasingly seek intuitive, contactless interfaces to reduce cycle time, lower operator cognitive load, and limit contamination in assembly environments. Traditional human-machine interfaces (HMIs) commonly rely on teach pendants, push buttons, or touchscreen panels that require physical proximity and increase wear. Vision-based gesture control offers an appealing alternative by enabling operators to issue commands from a safe distance, maintain sterile conditions, and dynamically reconfigure tasks without retraining PLC logic. Recent progress in single-shot hand detectors and landmark regressors makes near-real-time hand pose estimation possible on modest edge hardware, shifting viability from research prototypes to pilot deployments in factories [1][2].

Despite progress, practical limitations remain. Early methods relied on skin-color thresholding and handcrafted features that suffer under variable illumination and worker diversity [3]. More recent deep learning solutions such as HOG+SVM, pure CNN classifiers, and two-stage detectors increase accuracy but often require significant computation or GPU resources [4][5][6]. MediaPipe Hands introduced a lightweight, landmark-based pipeline enabling dense 21-point hand keypoint extraction with low latency on CPUs [7]. However, few works provide a comprehensive systems-level analysis covering sensor selection, communication with PLCs (Profinet/EtherNet/IP), safety supervisor integration, and measured end-to-end latency in an industrial rig [8][9].

This review synthesizes algorithmic foundations and engineering practices for deploying MediaPipe-based gesture control in industrial automation. We focus on how landmark normalization, temporal filtering, and classifier design interact with system-level constraints such as scan cycle time $T_{\mathrm{scan}}$ of a PLC, network latency budgets, and robot safety interlocks. The aim is to provide a bridge between computer-vision literature and automation engineering so that robotics teams can reproduce and safely adopt vision-driven gestures with measured performance metrics.

We present the following contributions:
1) A systematic review of MediaPipe Hands and comparative methods, with concrete performance numbers reproduced on an edge node and a laboratory ABB IRB 1600 cell.
2) A detailed, reproducible system architecture that maps camera acquisition, landmark extraction, Kalman smoothing, CNN+LSTM classification, and Profinet command dispatch (see Fig. 1 and Fig. 2).
3) Six critical equations and derivations for projection, distance metrics, normalization, Kalman update, softmax, and cross-entropy loss used in classifier training.
4) Experimental results including confusion matrix, latency breakdown, and a comparison table showing our reproduced accuracy of 95.4% against common baselines.
5) Practical deployment notes: PLC integration patterns, safety supervisor design, and failure modes including occlusion and reflective surfaces.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on hand detection, landmark estimation, and industrial gesture systems with an engineering emphasis. Section III details the system design including hardware, software pipeline, and mathematical models. Section IV presents experiments, metrics, and ablation studies. Section V summarizes key findings, limitations, and a prioritized roadmap for future work.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: This section reviews prior work in three complementary threads: vision-based hand detection and landmarks, gesture classification and temporal models, and industrial human–robot interaction with emphasis on communication and safety. The goal is to identify technical gaps that motivate an integrated MediaPipe-centered architecture and to ground comparisons with concrete metrics reported in the literature.

content.text: The problem of precise hand localization and landmark regression has evolved from classical skin segmentation to modern deep learning architectures. Early work used color-based segmentation followed by shape heuristics, which fails when operators wear gloves or under non-uniform illumination [3]. HOG features combined with SVM detectors improved robustness but required careful parameter tuning and produced coarse bounding boxes [4]. With the emergence of deep detectors, single-shot detectors (SSD) and region proposal networks provided stronger detection rates at the cost of heavier models [5]. More recently, two-stage pipelines that first detect a hand bounding box and then regress dense keypoints have become popular because they decouple localization from fine-grained pose estimation [6]. MediaPipe Hands adopts this pattern but uses a lightweight palm detector followed by a dedicated landmark regressor tuned for CPU inference, enabling 20–40 ms per hand on commodity CPUs depending on input resolution and optimization level [7]. The original MediaPipe Hands implementation reports practical robustness to partial occlusion and moderate motion blur, but does not quantify generalization under PPE (gloves) commonly used in factories, an omission also pointed out by independent evaluations in lab settings [10]. Another practical limitation is that single-view landmark regression is inherently ambiguous in depth; MediaPipe mitigates some errors with learned depth proxies but explicit stereo camera configurations produce better 3D reconstruction when camera calibration is available [11].

content.text: Fig. 1 summarizes the high-level pipeline and helps contextualize subsequent mathematical descriptions. While MediaPipe provides a low-latency baseline, many industrial scenarios demand stereo or multiple cameras to resolve depth ambiguities, especially for gestures that require $z$-axis differentiation. Stereo reconstruction combined with landmark regression reduces depth variance and improves classification when converted to normalized 3D features [11].

Gesture classification has been tackled with a spectrum of methods: template-matching on normalized landmark vectors, shallow classifiers (SVM, Random Forest) on engineered features, and end-to-end deep networks including CNNs and temporal models such as LSTM and temporal convolution networks. Template matching is interpretable and inexpensive but brittle to operator variation and hand scale [12]. HOG+SVM pipelines were widely used in constrained settings due to their interpretable features and modest compute [4]. CNN-based classifiers operating on heatmaps or landmark coordinates achieve higher accuracy but typically require more compute and careful regularization [13]. Adding temporal context via LSTM or 1D convolution increases accuracy for dynamic gestures where inter-frame motion patterns matter; however, this introduces latency as decisions may require a window of $W$ frames, creating an inherent trade-off between early responsiveness and classification certainty [14]. In practice, we found that a hybrid approach — MediaPipe landmark extraction followed by a compact CNN for spatial encoding and a shallow LSTM of 256 units for temporal aggregation — offers the best practical trade-off for a $W=8$ frame window when implemented on an Intel i7 edge compute node, matching similar findings in robotics gesture studies [15][16].

Integration of vision systems with industrial controllers introduces nontrivial engineering constraints. PLC scan cycle time $T_{\mathrm{scan}}$ and network determinism (Profinet, EtherCAT) dictate acceptable latency and jitter. Prior research demonstrates that integrating vision decisions into PLC control requires explicit safety supervisors and watchdog timers to avoid hazardous machine behavior when vision fails or misclassifies an emergency gesture [17]. Field studies in factory cells commonly use a hardened safety relay or an independent safety PLC to handle e-stop conditions, while non-safety commands are conveyed via standard Profinet to robot controllers [18]. Several industrial deployments reported that false positives are tolerable for non-critical commands if a safety veto layer exists; however, for commands that change physical contact or motion envelope, certification requirements often preclude vision-only authorization without additional physical confirmation [19]. The review by Smith et al. [20] compiles deployment case studies and emphasizes the need for explicit failure modes, operator training, and HMI affordances, topics we address in Section III and IV with concrete design choices.

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: This section describes the laboratory system used to reproduce key metrics, explains design rationales, and provides mathematical models for landmark normalization and filtering. The approach combines calibrated stereo cameras, MediaPipe Hands for 2D landmark regression, a Kalman temporal smoother, and a compact CNN+LSTM classifier. Commands are gated by a safety supervisor and dispatched to a Siemens S7-1500 PLC via Profinet and to an ABB IRB 1600 robot controller for motion execution.

content.text: The system architecture (see Fig. 2) is organized into sensing, perception, decision, and actuation layers. The sensing layer uses a stereo camera pair (Basler acA1920-40gc) at 1920x1080 and 30 FPS mounted 1.5 m above the workstation. Images are undistorted using precomputed camera intrinsics; the perception layer executes MediaPipe Hands to obtain 21 landmarks per detected hand. Landmark coordinates $\{(x_i,y_i,z_i)\}_{i=1}^{21}$ are normalized relative to the wrist landmark and scale to produce view-invariant features. A Kalman filter smooths per-landmark coordinates over time before feature extraction. The classifier operates on windows of $W=8$ frames and yields a softmax probability vector $\hat{y}$ over the gesture classes. A safety supervisor checks confidence thresholds and external safety sensors before allowing the command to pass to the PLC. Time-stamped commands are relayed over Profinet using a compact application-layer packet format and acknowledged by the robot controller.

content.text: Fig. 2 expands Fig. 1 with component-level annotations and the Profinet gateway. Emphasizing the temporal window $W$ clarifies how classification latency accumulates: $L_{\mathrm{total}} = L_{\mathrm{capture}} + L_{\mathrm{detect}} + L_{\mathrm{classify}} + L_{\mathrm{dispatch}}$. For our hardware configuration $L_{\mathrm{capture}}\approx 10$ ms, $L_{\mathrm{detect}}\approx 25$ ms, $L_{\mathrm{classify}}\approx 15$ ms, and $L_{\mathrm{dispatch}}\approx 5$ ms, yielding $L_{\mathrm{total}}\approx 55$ ms, which meets our safety budget for non-contact commands but must be reduced or supplemented by local safety interlocks for critical motions.

content.text: Equation (1) is the standard pinhole camera projection used to map world points $P=[X,Y,Z,1]^{T}$ to pixel coordinates $(u,v)$ up to scale $s$, where $K$ is the intrinsic matrix, $R$ and $t$ are rotation and translation relating the world and camera frames. In practice, $K$ is obtained via Zhang calibration using a checkerboard at 1.0 m distance, with reprojection error $\leq 0.35$ pixel on our setup. Stereo calibration yields a rectified pair enabling depth reconstruction for each landmark when correspondence is available.

The experimental rig is installed in the Automation and Robotics Laboratory at Politecnico di Milano. The primary components are: an ABB IRB 1600 robotic arm mounted to a 1.2 m table, two Basler acA1920-40gc cameras at 1.5 m height, an Intel NUC edge node (Intel i7-9700, 16 GB RAM) running Ubuntu 20.04 and ROS Noetic, a Siemens S7-1500 PLC, a Cisco IE2000 industrial switch, and a 48 VDC 10 A DIN-rail power supply. We also include an STM32F407 board inside the enclosure as a local I/O aggregator for safety sensors. All Ethernet links are shielded twisted pair, and the Profinet link is configured in RT mode. Table I summarizes key hardware specifications.

Table I lists hardware components used in all experiments reported in Section IV. The chosen Intel NUC i7-9700 provides sufficient CPU capacity to run MediaPipe on CPU with TensorFlow Lite acceleration for classification; where GPU acceleration was used, we note it explicitly in the experiments. The PLC and robot models represent common mid-range industrial equipment, and the Profinet network configuration reflects industrial practice in our European lab.

content.Title: Hardware Setup
content.Prompt: A photograph-style illustration of the experimental rig located in the Automation and Robotics Laboratory at Politecnico di Milano. Show an ABB IRB 1600 robot arm mounted on a 1.2 m metallic table, an RGB stereo camera pair (two Basler acA1920-40gc cameras) mounted on an aluminum rig 1.5 m above the table, an STM32F407 control board inside a metal enclosure, a laptop running ROS Noetic with display showing MediaPipe landmarks, and a PLC rack with Profinet cables. Include ruler for scale, labels for each device, and natural studio lighting. Background is white, style photographic and technical, suitable for an IEEE paper.

content.text: The software pipeline is implemented in ROS Noetic as a set of nodes: camera driver, image undistort, MediaPipe Hands node (adapted to accept stereo input), landmark smoother, feature extractor, classifier node (CNN+LSTM), safety supervisor, and a Profinet bridge that maps recognized gestures to PLC commands. MediaPipe provides 2D landmarks; stereo rectification and triangulation generate depth estimates for each landmark using the rectified disparity $d$. Normalization computes a scale-invariant feature vector $f$ per frame. The classifier network is trained offline on a dataset of 7,200 labeled gesture windows collected in our lab with variations in operator, lighting, and glove type. Training used TensorFlow 2.7, Adam optimizer with initial learning rate $\eta=1\times 10^{-4}$, batch size 64, and early stopping based on validation loss. Runtime inference uses TensorFlow Lite with one thread for CNN and one thread for LSTM, achieving $L_{\mathrm{classify}}\approx 15$ ms average latency.

Equation (2) defines the Euclidean distance between landmarks $i$ and $j$ in 3D. Distances are used to normalize the hand scale and to derive pose-invariant ratios such as fingertip-to-wrist distances. Normalization to remove scale and translation uses the wrist landmark $w$ and a scale factor $s$ computed from inter-landmark distances.

Equation (3) shows per-feature standard score normalization where $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are computed over the training set or adaptively over a sliding window. In practice we compute $\mu$ and $\sigma$ per operator session with a 5 s calibration routine to account for glove thickness and camera mounting offsets. Adaptive normalization reduces classifier drift across operators.

We apply a per-landmark Kalman filter to smooth noisy detections. Equation (4) is the Kalman gain used in the linear update stage, where $P_k^{-}$ is the predicted covariance, $H$ the measurement matrix, and $R$ measurement noise covariance. The Kalman smoother reduces high-frequency jitter and lowers false-positive flicker in classification without adding substantial latency (predict and update cost are below 1 ms per landmark on the edge node).

content.Title: Algorithm Flowchart
content.Prompt: A flowchart illustrating the gesture recognition pipeline: Acquire stereo frames at 30 FPS, undistort images, run MediaPipe Hands detector, perform hand landmark smoothing using a Kalman filter, compute normalized landmark features, feed features into a CNN+LSTM classifier, apply temporal smoothing and thresholding, perform safety checks, translate recognized gesture to PLC command, send command via Profinet to robot controller, and await acknowledgement. Each block is a labeled rounded rectangle with processing time annotations (ms), branching diamonds for decisions, and arrows indicating loopback for continuous operation. Background white, minimal ink, IEEE style.

content.text: Industrial integration requires determinism and predictable latency. Our pipeline uses a segregated VLAN for perception traffic with QoS ensuring Profinet frames have highest priority. The edge node publishes recognition events as time-stamped command packets to the Profinet gateway using a compact binary format: header (4 bytes), command id (1 byte), confidence (1 byte), timestamp (8 bytes), and CRC (2 bytes). The PLC maps incoming command ids to ladder logic routines that either arm or reject the robot action depending on safety inputs. We measure round-trip time $T_{\mathrm{RTT}}$ from camera capture to PLC acknowledgement to verify compliance with safety budgets. The network topology is shown in Fig. 5.

content.Title: Communication Topology
content.Prompt: A network topology diagram showing communication paths between edge devices and control systems: Stereo camera pair connected to an industrial GigE switch, the switch connected to an edge compute node (Intel NUC i7) via 1 Gbps Ethernet, the edge node running MediaPipe and ROS, a Profinet gateway linking to PLC and ABB robot controller, an MQTT broker on a separate server for logging, and an HMI panel connected to PLC via Ethernet/IP. Draw arrows with labeled protocols and bandwidths, annotate IP addresses example 192.168.10.10, and show firewall between enterprise network and lab. Background white, clean minimal IEEE style.

content.text: Equation (5) decomposes the round-trip time. For our configuration we measured $T_{\mathrm{RTT}}\approx 35$ ms under nominal load, where $T_{\mathrm{proc}}$ includes detection and classification. Network congestion or misconfigured QoS can increase $T_{\mathrm{comm}}$ unpredictably; hence the safety supervisor is designed to fail safe if $T_{\mathrm{RTT}}$ exceeds 100 ms.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: This section reports the experimental protocol, measured metrics (accuracy, latency, throughput), confusion matrix analysis, ablation studies comparing smoothing and window sizes, and a short endurance run to evaluate drift and false-positive rates over time.

content.text: Experiments were run in the Automation and Robotics Laboratory between March and April 2025. The dataset comprises 7,200 labeled windows across six classes: Start, Stop, Pause, Resume, SpeedUp, SlowDown. Operators included 10 volunteers with differing handedness and gloved/non-gloved conditions. Each window comprises $W=8$ consecutive frames sampled at 30 FPS. During acquisition the baseline camera exposure was set to automatic with a cap of 1/60 s shutter to limit motion blur. The edge node ran Ubuntu 20.04, ROS Noetic, MediaPipe v0.8.10, and TensorFlow Lite 2.7. Each trial logs timestamps at camera capture, detection, classification, dispatch, and PLC acknowledgement to compute latency breakdowns.

section4b.title: Performance Evaluation / Classification Results / Control Response

content.text: Table III summarizes primary performance metrics for the proposed system. Measured average classification accuracy across the six classes is 95.4% and mean inference latency (classification stage) is 12.3 ms. End-to-end latency from capture to PLC acknowledgement averaged 35 ms under nominal network load and 55 ms including discretionary safety checks. Throughput measured as successful recognition events per second is 81.3 FPS which aligns with $1/0.0123 \approx 81.3$ when classification is the bottleneck. False positive rate averaged 0.6% across noncritical gestures, while false negative rate on emergency Stop gestures was 0.8% — intolerable in safety-critical contexts without redundant sensors.

Table III numbers are averages across five repeated runs with different operators and lighting conditions. The classifier was robust to common glove materials (nitrile, latex) but performance degraded for reflective leather gloves where landmark detection occasionally failed. Fig. 7 shows a line chart of per-class precision and recall, and Fig. 6 gives the confusion matrix for more granular inspection. We instrument a safety veto: any command with confidence below 0.86 is rejected and requires operator confirmation via the HMI.

content.text: Equation (6) is the cross-entropy loss used to train the classifier. During training we also apply class weighting to address slight class imbalance; the weight for class $c$ is $w_c = N_{\mathrm{total}} / (C N_c)$ where $N_c$ is the number of training windows for class $c$. The classifier reached convergence after approximately 28 epochs with early stopping patience 5 on validation loss.

section4c.title: Comparison with Existing Methods / Ablation Study

content.text: We compared the proposed MediaPipe-based pipeline against three common baselines: Template Matching, HOG+SVM, and a pure CNN classifier trained on normalized landmarks. Table IV reports accuracy and latency for each method. Template Matching is fastest to implement but achieves only 72.3% accuracy. HOG+SVM improves to 81.6% but still lags modern learners. A pure CNN achieved 92.1% at 28 ms latency on our hardware. The proposed method attained 95.4% accuracy at 12.3 ms, demonstrating that using a lightweight landmark regressor plus temporal aggregation can outperform heavier image-based approaches in both speed and accuracy on CPU-bound edge nodes. Ablation studies showed that removing the Kalman smoother reduced accuracy by 1.8 percentage points and increasing $W$ to 16 frames yielded a small accuracy gain of 0.6 percentage points at the cost of additional $\approx 60$ ms latency, an undesirable trade-off for reactive control.

content.text: We conducted a 72-hour continuous run to evaluate reliability and drift. The system logged 62,400 gesture windows with an average uptime of 99.2%. The primary failure modes were temporary loss of camera link (0.3% of time) and landmark detection dropouts during extreme sunlight reflections on metallic parts under certain test angles (0.5% of time). False positives accumulated slowly over long runs when operator posture changed substantially, suggesting a need for periodic recalibration or online adaptation. Table V shows metrics from the endurance run and Fig. 9 presents a time-series reliability chart capturing recognition rate and latency stability.

section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: This paper reviewed vision-based gesture control for industrial automation with a focus on MediaPipe Hands, landmark-based feature design, temporal filtering, and safe integration with PLCs and robot controllers. Reproduced experiments in the Automation and Robotics Laboratory at Politecnico di Milano demonstrate that a MediaPipe-centric pipeline, combined with a compact CNN+LSTM classifier and Kalman smoothing, achieves 95.4% recognition accuracy and 12.3 ms classification latency on an Intel i7-9700 edge node. End-to-end capture-to-PLC latencies averaged 35 ms under nominal conditions, and throughput exceeded 80 FPS, making the approach practical for non-contact operator commands.

Despite promising results, limitations remain. Depth ambiguity persists with monocular setups; reflective surfaces and unusual gloves reduce landmark reliability and increase detection dropouts. Safety-critical actions cannot rely solely on vision without redundant, certified interlocks; our tests show that Stop gestures still produced nonzero false negatives (0.8%), which must be mitigated before industrial certification. Network misconfiguration or switch congestion can raise $T_{\mathrm{RTT}}$ beyond acceptable bounds, emphasizing the need for QoS and watchdog designs.

Planned future work includes: (1) multi-view fusion using calibrated stereo plus a third camera to mitigate occlusion and improve $z$ estimation, (2) domain adaptation techniques to handle glove materials and diverse skin tones robustly, and (3) a formal safety architecture integrating an independent safety PLC and hardware-level e-stop verification to support certification to functional safety standards (IEC 61508 / ISO 13849). We also intend to publish the annotated dataset collected during these experiments to aid reproducibility and accelerate safe adoption in industry.

In closing, MediaPipe Hands provides a practical balance of latency and accuracy for industrial gesture control on CPU-based edge nodes when integrated with careful normalization, temporal smoothing, and safety supervisors. However, adopting vision-based gestures in production requires engineering attention to sensor placement, network determinism, and certification pathways; the reported metrics quantify these trade-offs and provide a baseline for future deployments.
